book.title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
book.author: John C. Bogle

confidence_note: Needle-in-haystack line and cost arithmetic are well attested; no concrete case in the book was verified for this idea, so the story stays short and concept-based. The old text's SPIVA claim and 'winners erase losers' wording were not verified and dropped.
facts: Bogle says picking a mutual fund that will beat the stock market over the long term is, in Cervantes' observation, like looking for a needle in a haystack.
His corollary: 'Don't look for the needle in the haystack. Just buy the haystack!'
A broad index fund owns the whole market, the haystack, instead of trying to pick which stocks win.
His arithmetic: gross return minus costs equals net return; investors as a group earn the market's return before costs and less after them.
Active funds spend on research and trading, and that expense comes out of the investors' returns; the index fund's cost is low.
The book's subtitle promises 'the only way to guarantee your fair share of stock market returns'.
scene_details: a haystack with a needle in it
a single subtraction: gross return minus costs
tension: The effort of finding the needle is paid for by the very people hoping for it.
opening_idea: Open on the needle in the haystack and who pays for the search.

lessons.idea: If you cannot pick the winner ahead of time, owning everything and paying little is a sound plan.

reflect_final: Where in your life do you pay someone to find the needle, and what would it look like to settle for the haystack?

use_cases.situation: A colleague pitches a stock tip over coffee
use_cases.move: Say: Bogle's line is don't look for the needle, buy the haystack. What makes this the needle?
Check what the fund holds and costs; if you pay someone to pick, ask what they do that the whole market does not.

use_cases.situation: Advising a family member new to investing
use_cases.move: Explain it as gross return minus costs equals net return, and look at costs first.

pocket_idea: The search for the one winning fund is paid for out of your returns; owning the whole haystack skips the search.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Bogle's advice on picking a winning fund: don't look for the needle, buy the haystack.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Bogle borrows Cervantes' needle in a haystack for picking winning funds and answers: buy the haystack, own the market, and pay little for it.
